descriptionChirho: Qal stative/intransitive sense: a situation, action, or state 'is good' or 'is pleasing' to someone. Arabic consistently uses حَسُنَ (ḥasuna, 'be good/beautiful') and يَحْسُنُ (yaḥsunu) for this sense, distinguishing it from the 'glad heart' sense which uses طَابَ (ṭāba). Korean renders with stative 좋다 forms (좋으면, 좋으리라, 좋은) rather than causative constructions. Swahili uses stative -kuwa vizuri ('be good') and -pendeza ('be pleasing') without causative -isha derivation. Covers all Qal imperfect, consecutive imperfect, and conjunctive imperfect forms expressing the idea 'it is/was/will be good/pleasing/well'.

Qal sense specifically of the heart or spirit being glad, merry, in good spirits. Arabic distinctly uses طَابَ (ṭāba, 'be pleasant/delightful') rather than حَسُنَ, revealing a genuine Semitic semantic distinction: this is not abstract 'goodness' but experiential gladness. Korean renders 좋았다 but context is emotional. Swahili consistently uses -furahi ('rejoice') and moyo ukafurahi ('heart rejoiced') — the derivational shift from -kuwa vizuri to -furahi confirms a distinct sense. Spanish uses alegrarse ('rejoice') rather than ser bueno.

labelChirho: Hifil: do good to, treat well
descriptionChirho: Core Hifil causative meaning: actively doing good to someone, treating someone well, bestowing benefit. Arabic uses the Form IV أَحْسَنَ (aḥsana) / يُحْسِنُ (yuḥsinu, 'do well/do good') — the standard Arabic causative of ح-س-ن. Korean uses 선대하다 ('treat well'), 선을 행하다 ('practice goodness'), 잘 대하다 ('treat well'). Swahili uses -tendea mema ('do good to') and -fanya mema ('do good') — the applicative -tendea confirms a benefactive/transitive action directed at someone. Covers all Hifil finite forms (perfect, imperfect, imperative, jussive, participle, consecutive) expressing the sense 'do good / treat well / act rightly toward someone'.

Hifil infinitive absolute used adverbially to mean 'well, thoroughly, clearly, rightly.' Arabic renders with adverbial جَيِّدًا (jayyidan, 'well/good') and إِحْسَانًا (iḥsānan, 'doing good') — both adverbial accusatives, not finite verbs. Korean uses bare adverbs 잘 ('well'), 완전히 ('completely'), 반드시 ('certainly'). Swahili uses vizuri ('well'), kabisa ('completely'), hakika ('indeed'). This is a grammaticalized adverbial function distinct from the finite 'do good' sense, as confirmed by the cross-linguistic convergence on adverbs rather than verb phrases.

Hifil sense of correcting, improving, making something right or better. Arabic crucially uses أَصْلَحَ (aṣlaḥa) / تُصْلِحُونَ (tuṣliḥūna) from root ص-ل-ح ('repair, reform, put right') — a completely different Arabic root from أَحْسَنَ, proving this is a genuinely distinct sense in Semitic. Korean uses 바르게 하다 ('make right') alongside 좋게 하다. Swahili uses -tengeneza ('repair, fix, put in order') rather than -fanya mema ('do good'), and -boresha ('improve'). Spanish uses mejorar ('improve') rather than hacer bien ('do good').

Hifil sense of adorning or beautifying, applied to personal appearance. Arabic uses وَزَيَّنَتْ (wa-zayyaant, Form II of ز-ي-ن 'adorn/beautify') — an entirely different Arabic root from both أَحْسَنَ and أَصْلَحَ, confirming a distinct lexical sense. Korean 꾸몄다 ('decorated/adorned'). Swahili -pamba ('decorate, adorn'). Spanish adornar. This specialized meaning of יטב Hifil applies to making oneself attractive.

Hifil sense of performing music skillfully, playing an instrument well. Arabic أَحْسِنُوا (aḥsinū) / أَحْسِنِي (aḥsinī) remains within the ح-س-ن root but the collocational context (with instruments) creates a specialized sense. Korean 잘 ('well') in musical context. Swahili uses -piga vizuri ('strike/play well') — the verb -piga ('strike/hit') confirms instrumental/musical performance. Spanish tocar bien ('play well'). This is a domain-specific application of 'do well' that lexicographically merits separation.

Hifil sense of causing joy, making merry, cheering someone. Arabic يُسَرِّونَ (yusarrūna, Form II of س-ر-ر 'cause joy/gladness') for the participial form, and يِطِيبْكَ (yiṭībka, 'make pleasant to you') from ط-ي-ب for the personal-object form — both different from أَحْسَنَ. Korean 즐겁게 하다 ('make joyful') and 좋게 하게 하라 ('cause to make good'). Swahili -furahisha ('cause to rejoice') — the causative -isha suffix on -furahi confirms the causative-of-emotion reading. This is the Hifil counterpart to the Qal 'be glad' sense.

Specialized Hifil sense of tending or trimming lamps in the tabernacle/temple. Arabic بِإِصلاحِهِ (bi-iṣlāḥihi, 'when he repairs/maintains it') from root ص-ل-ح in its concrete 'maintenance' meaning. Korean 손질하다 ('tend, groom, maintain'). Swahili -tayarisha ('prepare, make ready'). Spanish aderezar ('trim, prepare'). This is a technical priestly term for lamp maintenance, distinct from general 'do good' or 'improve'.

Hifil sense used comparatively: 'be better than,' 'surpass in goodness.' Arabic هَلْ أَنْتِ أَحْسَنُ (hal anti aḥsanu, 'are you better?') using the elative/comparative أَحْسَنُ form of ح-س-ن. Korean 더 좋으냐 ('are you better?'). Swahili bora kuliko ('better than') — uses the comparative kuliko construction. Spanish mejor ('better'). The comparative semantics are grammaticalized differently from simple 'do good.'

Hifil participle describing those who march stately or go with a fine gait. Arabic حَسَنو (ḥasanū, 'those good of') — adjectival rather than verbal. Korean 좋게 걷다/가다 ('walk/go well'). Swahili vyenye mwendo mzuri / hatua nzuri ('those with a good gait / fine step') — the nominal mwendo ('gait') and hatua ('step') confirm this is about manner of movement. Spanish los que marchan bien ('those who march well'). A specialized participial sense combining motion with quality.

Hifil impersonal construction meaning 'it seems good (to someone),' used for approval or decision-making. Arabic يَرْضَى (yarḍā, 'he is pleased/approves') from root ر-ض-ي ('be pleased, approve') — a completely different Arabic root signaling the evaluative/approval nuance rather than moral 'doing good.' Korean 좋게 여기다 ('regard as good'). Swahili -pendeza ('be pleasing'). Spanish parecer bien ('seem good'). The Arabic root shift to ر-ض-ي proves this is a distinct sense of subjective evaluation/approval.
